stem: Follow Nell's feeling from the start of the text to the end. Which choice best describes how it changes?
stimulus:
The following text is from an original short story. Nell keeps the wage ledger at a small shoe factory.

Nell had dreaded the first of the month for a year. Every payday the columns came out short, and every payday she had to tell someone that their hours had been cut. This month she added the totals twice, then a third time, not trusting them. The new contract had raised every rate. She closed the ledger, smoothed its cover with both hands, and found that she was smiling.
choices: Nell moves from dreading payday to feeling relieved about the higher wages.
Nell moves from feeling relieved about payday to dreading the higher wages.
Nell adds the totals three times because she doubts her own arithmetic skills.
Nell hides the new totals so that the workers will not ask for even more.
explanation: Find where the feeling starts and where it ends. At the start, Nell 'had dreaded the first of the month.' At the end, she 'found that she was smiling' after the new contract raised every rate. So her feeling goes from dread to relief. This one step, following a character's feeling from the first line to the last, is what you need for the Easy main-idea question on fiction excerpts. That question asks which choice best states the main idea, and its answer always matches the direction the feeling moves.

B.why: You picked up the right two feelings but put them in the wrong order. The dread comes first and the smile comes last. When you check the direction of a feeling, look at the final sentence to see where it ends up.

C.why: She does add the totals three times, but that is one line from the middle of the text, and it is about not trusting good news, not about her arithmetic. A choice built on one sentence leaves out how her feeling changes from start to end.

D.why: The text never says Nell hides anything or worries about the workers asking for more. You added a motive the text does not give. If you can't point to the line that says it, the choice is wrong.

stem: Restate the whole poem in plain words, including the turn at the end. Which choice best describes what the speaker feels by the last line?
stimulus:
The following text is from an original poem. The speaker remembers the swifts that nested in a chimney nearby.

All summer the swifts stitched the sky above the chimney,
thin black arcs too quick to count.
I meant to learn them: where they slept, how far they flew.
Now the chimney is quiet, the evenings cold,
and only now, with the sky empty,
do I wish I had watched them longer.
choices: The speaker describes swifts flying in quick black arcs above a chimney.
The speaker is glad that the swifts have gone and the evenings are quiet.
The speaker regrets not watching the swifts more closely before they left.
The speaker avoids the chimney because the swifts flew too close to it.
explanation: In plain words, the poem says: 'All summer swifts flew over the chimney. I meant to study them. Now they're gone, and only now do I wish I had watched them longer.' The words 'only now' and 'wish' mark the turn, and that turn is the feeling the poem ends on: regret. On the Easy main-idea question about a poem, the answer comes from this turn and not from the opening images.

A.why: This is true of the first two lines only. You stopped at the images and missed the 'only now… do I wish' turn at the end, which is where the poem says what it means.

B.why: This reverses the tone. The quiet chimney and the empty sky are things the speaker misses, not things the speaker celebrates. 'Wish' tells you the feeling is regret.

D.why: The poem never says the speaker avoids anything or was bothered by the birds. You added a motive the text doesn't give.

stem: Follow Tomás's feeling from the start of the text to the end. Which choice best describes how he feels about his work?
stimulus:
The following text is from an original short story. Tomás is an apprentice in a printmaking workshop.

Tomás had meant to carve only the border before lunch. But the cherry block took the gouge so cleanly that he kept going, curl after pale curl, into the leaves and then the bird's wing. He did not hear the bell or notice the light shift across the bench. When the master finally touched his shoulder, the windows were dark, and Tomás looked up, surprised to find the day gone.
choices: Tomás is bored by the carving and keeps waiting for the long day to end.
Tomás is so absorbed in the carving that he loses all track of the time.
Tomás carves well past dark so that he can hide his work from the master.
Tomás carves a block of cherry wood that shows a bird among some leaves.
explanation: Follow the feeling from start to end. Tomás meant to stop at lunch, but he 'kept going,' did not hear the bell, and was 'surprised to find the day gone.' Each detail shows the same thing: he is absorbed in the work. On the Easy main-idea question about fiction, the answer matches a feeling like this, one that the details build up together.

A.why: This reverses the tone. Someone who is bored watches the clock, but Tomás didn't hear the bell at all. Missing the time is a sign that he is absorbed, not that he is waiting for the day to end.

C.why: Nothing in the text says Tomás is hiding anything. The master walks up and touches his shoulder. You added a motive the text never gives.

D.why: This is a true detail, but it only tells you what he carved, not how he feels while carving. It leaves out the feeling that the whole passage builds toward.

stem: Follow the narrator's feeling from the start of the text to the end. Which choice best describes how it changes?
stimulus:
The following text is from an original memoir. The narrator is a marine biologist returning to a coral reef two years after a heat wave bleached it white.

I dropped into the water expecting a graveyard. Two years earlier the reef had been bone-white from end to end, and I had stopped telling people I studied it. However, near the base of the old brain corals, I found small brown knobs, new polyps, no bigger than my thumbnail. I counted forty before my air ran low. I surfaced laughing into my mask, already planning the next dive.
choices: The narrator expects to find a recovering reef but is let down by its damage.
The narrator dives on a reef that was bleached white by a heat wave long ago.
The narrator concludes that the reef has fully healed and needs no more study.
The narrator expects to find a dead reef but grows hopeful on seeing regrowth.
explanation: The word 'However' marks the turn. Before it, the narrator expects 'a graveyard.' After it, the narrator finds new polyps and surfaces 'laughing,' already planning to come back. So the feeling goes from expecting the worst to feeling hopeful. On the Easy main-idea question about memoirs and stories, the answer usually follows whatever comes after a pivot like this one.

A.why: This swaps the expectation and the outcome. The narrator expected damage and found regrowth, not the other way around. Check which side of 'However' each feeling is on.

B.why: This comes from the italic introduction and the first two sentences only. It sets the scene, but it leaves out the change of feeling, which is the point of the passage.

C.why: Forty small polyps is a hopeful sign, not a full recovery. The narrator is already planning the next dive, which is the opposite of 'no more study.' This choice claims more than the text supports.

stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is from a short story about Ines, who has just finished her first week of work at a textile mill.

At the gate, the foreman handed Ines a brown envelope. She did not open it on the tram. At home she set it on the kitchen table and counted the coins twice, lining them up by size. Six days of threading bobbins, and here they were, small and solid. She sat back and smiled, feeling for the first time that her work was worth something.
choices: Ines feels proud when she receives the wages from her first week of work.
Ines feels let down by how small the wages from her first week of work are.
Ines keeps her first week's wages hidden so that no one else can take them.
Ines notices that the coins in her pay envelope come in different sizes.
explanation: The introduction tells you who Ines is and what is happening: she has just finished her first week at the mill. Now follow her feelings from start to end. She counts the coins carefully, she smiles, and the last sentence names the feeling directly: her work is 'worth something.' That is pride, and choice A covers both the situation (her first wages) and where her emotion ends up. This is the basic move behind every literary main-idea question: work out the situation, then follow the character's feeling to the end.

B.why: You took the word 'small' as a complaint and flipped the tone. The coins are 'small and solid,' and Ines smiles. Nothing in the text shows disappointment. Choices that reverse the character's feeling are the most common trap in this kind of question.

C.why: You added a motive the text never gives. Ines waits to open the envelope until she gets home, but the passage never says she is hiding it or worried that someone will take it. If you can't point to a line that states the motive, the choice is adding something the text doesn't say.

D.why: This is true, since she lines the coins up by size, but it describes only one small action. The passage is about what the wages mean to her. A choice can be accurate and still be too narrow to be the main idea.
